title: Lift up your heads (Luke 21:5–28)
hook: wars and signs; but when these things begin, look up

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow's two lepta, more than they all. Your line was out of her poverty.

Some people in the temple courts are admiring the building, and it deserved it: huge pale stones, gifts hung on the walls, a sanctuary still being finished and enlarged after decades of work. Jesus looks at the same walls and says the days are coming when not one stone will be left upon another. His friends want details. When? What sign? He doesn't give a date. He gives a long list of frightening things, and then an instruction about where to point your eyes.

The list is hard to hear. Wars and commotions. Nation against nation. Earthquakes, famines, plagues. Arrests and betrayals, even by family. Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Signs in the sun, moon and stars, and the sea roaring. Yet threaded through it are calm sentences: "Be not terrified." "There shall not an hair of your head perish. In your patience possess ye your souls." Then the turn: "And then shall they see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh." When the news is terrible, the natural thing is to duck, to hunch, to stare at the ground. He tells them to stand up straight and look up. Redemption, apolytrosis, was a word for buying back a captive or a slave: release, coming toward you. Christians read this chapter in more than one way. Part of it, many say, came true within a generation: in the year seventy, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. Part of it, most Christians say, still waits for the day Christ returns. Some read nearly all of it as fulfilled; others nearly all as future. Some have tried to pull dates out of it, but the chapter never gives one. It gives a posture: when the world shakes, lift your head.
screen: `THE YEAR SEVENTY, AND THE DAY TO COME.`
then, large: `LOOK UP, AND LIFT UP YOUR HEADS.`

segments.voice: Notice your posture right now; if you've been scrolling, your head is probably bent and your shoulders curled. Breathe out, lift your chin a little, let your shoulders drop back, and look up at the ceiling or out at the sky for a few breaths. Hold one thing that frightens you with your head up instead of down, and if you pray, bring it to God from there.
Apolytrosis, Greek for redemption, release by a ransom paid: not duck and hide, but stand straight and look up.
Your line: your redemption draws near. Release, coming toward you, not away. Day five hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Many churches read Jesus's words about the end in the season of Advent, when Christians prepare both for Christmas and for Christ's return, and they pray in the creeds that he will come again.

chat.says: The news feels like the end of the world. What did Jesus tell people to do then?
options: Look up and lift your heads; he said be not terrified, redemption draws near.
Keep your head down and stay quiet until the bad news passes.
Be afraid; fear is the right answer when the world shakes like that.
chat.meaning: Amid wars and signs he says be not terrified, then: look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.

apolytrosis.meaning: Greek for redemption: a captive bought back

Son of man.meaning: the title Jesus uses for the one coming in a cloud

sanctuary.meaning: the temple's holy building, still being enlarged

sources.quoted: there shall not an hair of your head perish. In your patience possess ye your souls.

And then shall they see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.

notes: Destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by Rome in AD 70. Confirm the 'within about forty years' phrasing in the myth reveal (depends on dating the crucifixion around AD 30–33).
Herod's temple enlargement continued for decades (cf. John 2:20, 'forty and six years'). Hook says 'still being finished and enlarged'; confirm.
Readings described without ranking: partly fulfilled in AD 70 and partly future (common), mostly fulfilled (preterist), mostly future (futurist). Confirm the labels are fair.
Luke 21:18 sits alongside 21:16 ('some of you shall they cause to be put to death'); the script quotes 18–19 as calm sentences without claiming physical safety. Confirm.

Audit (second sample): removed the overstatement that no reader finds a timetable in Luke 21 (date-setters have tried); replaced the fork distractor 'run to the mountains', which Jesus actually says in Luke 21:21.
